articles.title: Today’s irreverent politics ignore ancient wisdom: The need to know your limits
articles.author: Robert A. Ballingall, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Maine
paras: A common complaint today laments the “shamelessness” of politicians. Until recently, the argument goes, more elected officials had a sense of shame to hold them back from ugly words and deeds, at least in public. Many in the current crop, however, seem to have no fear of disgrace; they revel in contempt for the niceties of old – unwritten rules against cursing, slander or lying, but also written rules against abuse of power.
The problem isn’t so much a question of bad manners or even of corruption. It’s really about leadership.

I study the history of political thought and work on the psychology of lawfulness: the character traits citizens need for the rule of law to work. One such trait is each person’s ability to limit herself – to revere some larger principle that she would be ashamed to betray.

That’s all the more true for good leaders, even in a constitutional republic defined by checks and balances. Sometimes decisions need to be made over the objections of partisan opposition or of another branch of government. But the public can trust decision-makers only if those leaders check themselves.

Like many problems, political shamelessness may seem new, but thinkers stretching back to the ancient Greeks have warned of its perils, which they described as “irreverence” – the failure to respect something bigger than ourselves. If today’s politics seem threatened by some such menace, it may be because we are neglecting this ancient wisdom.
Perhaps the most searching account of this problem and what to do about it can be found in a work by the Greek philosopher Plato, who died in 347 B.C.E. The text is known simply as the “Laws.”

Like his better-known “Republic,” the “Laws” envisions a “city in speech”: a utopia, a place that exists only in theory. But whereas the city of the “Republic” is ruled autocratically by “philosopher kings,” the “Laws” explores the possibilities and limitations of what is now called constitutional government.

All of Plato’s writings suggest that the most significant political fact is the scarcity of wisdom: the dearth of knowledge needed to live a flourishing human life. What’s more, he taught, most of us don’t recognize our own ignorance – indeed, we powerfully resist recognizing it.

Plato’s “Laws” examines the rule of law in light of this fact. It teaches that the function of law is to awaken citizens and politicians to their own ignorance and then to point them to a wise, ethical authority.
At its best, law wouldn’t just protect security or individual rights. It would provoke people to recognize their profound need of a standard of good and bad beyond their own judgment.

Otherwise, human nature being what it is, Plato saw that each person would corruptly “honor his own” – himself and everything connected to him – “more than the truth.” He would rationalize his own prejudices and justify his own selfishness.

In the “Laws,” the antidote to this problem is what Plato calls “aidos,” or reverence: the virtue governing shame, as well as awe. Taken by themselves, shame and awe are neither laudable nor blameworthy. But to have reverence, Plato suggests, is to feel these emotions for the right reasons.

Shame and awe go together for Plato because they both involve a feeling of diminishment: a sense of our own limits. With shame, this feeling is social, connected to the fear of someone else’s disapproving gaze. With awe, the feeling of smallness is inspired by something that makes our own concerns and capacities seem trivial – something like God or the divine.

It might seem as though a virtuous person would not feel shame; she would simply never do or say anything shameful. But in Plato’s eyes, precious few achieve so pure a virtue. For most, fear of shame is a necessary backstop to push people away from what wrongly tempts them. Likewise, awe prevents people from underestimating difficult tasks or from overestimating themselves.

According to the “Laws,” the proper object of reverence is wisdom, represented as God: “the measure of all things.” The text stresses the awesome nature of the wisdom needed to judge things well – the need to look for truth outside ourselves. It teaches that we should be ashamed to “measure” things by reference only to our own fallible judgment.

Reverence might seem irrelevant to modern politics. In liberal democracies, public life is devoted to securing liberty, not to learning virtue. Shaming people for disregarding the awesome nature of wisdom might appear a gross violation of their freedom of conscience. Modern societies can scarcely agree on what is shameful to begin with.

Reverence might also seem to involve a piety that is out of place in a diverse democracy. Many people believe in God, but political decisions are judged by secular standards like their popularity, or by whether they benefit the public interest.

Nevertheless, I would argue that modern politics continue to depend on something akin to reverence. Liberal democracies might not use government to teach virtue directly, but they do need citizens and statesmen who appreciate the limits of their own judgment and their need of higher principles to guide their decisions.

It helps that awe need not be inspired by gods – or wisdom, which was what Plato truly revered. Citizens might feel awe, for example, at the enormous responsibility of self-government. As philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote in the 18th century, democracy is more suited to gods than men: rightly understood, it is demanding in the highest degree.

Modern liberty is especially demanding; it isn’t only a matter of having a right to vote or speak our minds, as important as such rights may be. It is also a matter of having to choose between myriad ethical, religious and cultural traditions, or to choose none at all.
Such freedom is both a boon and a burden. In today’s democracies, citizens are responsible for their own ethical lives: for determining what should count as right and wrong, good and bad.

But it is precisely because we are free to waste our freedom, Plato might say, that we need reverence all the more: feeling awe for the responsibility of using that freedom well, and shame when we do not. As for political leaders, until they cease to find an approving audience for their contempt of principled behavior, the shamelessness that many observers find so disturbing will likely continue.

articles.title: Across the US, people don’t want data centers coming to their communities
articles.author: Neha Gour, Ph.D. Candidate in Science Communication, George Mason University
paras: Regardless of their views on politics or climate change, most Americans oppose the development of data centers in their communities.

These large buildings filled with computers that store and process digital information, increasingly to support various applications of artificial intelligence, are being built rapidly across the United States. They can bring economic investment and jobs, but the pollution created by generating the electricity they need can also harm public health, pollute air, use up water, create noise and raise energy costs.

As more data centers are proposed, some local communities are pushing back against new and prospective projects. These debates are already influencing local zoning and permitting decisions, and increasingly reaching state lawmakers.

In early September, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey issued an executive order that no state agency will issue permits for data center development unless the project already has local approval from the municipality where it will be located. In Vermont, where Gov. Phil Scott vetoed a bill that would have imposed strict regulations on data centers, local governments are taking matters into their own hands by banning data centers in their towns.
Public opinion is playing an important role in shaping how data center expansion unfolds across the country.

We are researchers studying science communication, climate change and public health. To better understand what Americans think about these issues, we examined data from the Spring 2026 Climate Change in the American Mind survey. It is a nationally representative survey of adults in the U.S. conducted by the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and the George Mason University Center for Climate Change Communication. Our findings align with other recent polling on the topic.
Most Americans oppose a data center in their area

In an April 2026 survey of 1,068 adults, 930 of whom are registered voters, we and our research colleagues Jennifer Carman, Seth Rosenthal, Anthony Leiserowitz and Edward Maibach asked respondents the degree to which they would support or oppose building a data center in their local area.
Just over half – 56% – said they would oppose it, while only 15% said they would support it.

The opposition is not limited to one political group. A majority of Americans in most groups across the political continuum said they oppose the development of data centers in their communities, although the extent of that opposition varies somewhat between groups.
Among registered voters, about three-quarters of liberal Democrats and about half of conservative Republicans said they oppose having a data center built in their local area.
People’s perspectives on climate change

For a closer look at how people view data centers, we built on our past work about Americans’ views about global warming and actions to reduce climate change and its effects. That research has identified six distinct groups of views on those issues, which we call “the Six Americas.”

Opposition to local data centers is highest among those in the Alarmed category, those most worried about climate change – 71% of whom opposed data centers being built in their community. But opposition is also very strong among those in the Dismissive category, who reject the idea that global warming is happening and human-caused.
These findings show that Americans with widely different beliefs about global warming can nonetheless hold similar views about local data center development.
Most Americans expect data centers to increase their electricity bills

Electricity costs are a major concern Americans have about data centers, particularly amid broader concerns about the increasing cost of living. Agreements between power companies and data center owners aren’t always clear about who will pay to generate the massive amounts of electricity involved – and it may be functionally impossible to tell if the costs are shared fairly.

A majority of Americans, 59%, expect their electricity bills to increase if a data center opens in their local area. Just 5% think their bills would decrease; 25% said they don’t know. The remaining 12% said they don’t expect their bills to be affected.
Concern about higher electricity bills is bipartisan. Among registered voters, majorities of every political group expect their bills to increase.

Electricity cost worries also span all views on climate change. The only group where a majority didn’t expect a data center to raise their power bills was the Disengaged, who don’t pay much attention to or hear about climate change very often, of whom 43% reported that expectation. But about as many of that group, 42%, said they didn’t know what might happen to their electric bills.
Most Americans support requiring data centers to offset their electricity use

We also asked Americans about one idea to address the large amount of electricity used by data centers: Instead of building new power plants to provide additional electricity, an advocacy group called Rewiring America has proposed that data center developers could be required to install rooftop solar and help weatherize and insulate nearby homes whose owners want these improvements. Those changes could generate new electricity and save additional energy to help provide the power the data center needs.
Respondents strongly supported making this idea a state or local requirement.

This proposal has considerable public support, from across the political spectrum and among the various Six Americas groups of views on climate change. Only the Dismissive group – those who dismiss the idea that climate change is happening – saw less than half of its members support these policies, even though majorities of that group oppose having a data center nearby and expect a local data center to increase their electricity bills. This is consistent with their tendency to oppose renewable energy development more generally.

The companies leading the AI boom are seeking not only computer servers, electricity and land, but also public support. As data centers continue to expand across the country, understanding Americans’ views on them, and what people expect from developers, is becoming increasingly important.
Our research shows that Americans with very different political views and opinions about global warming can share similar views about data center development.
Some state regulators and utility companies are already considering structuring electricity rates to prevent data center costs from being passed on to other customers.
At the same time, the differences matter, especially in terms of specific policies that may or may not be broadly popular.
For policymakers, data center developers and community leaders, understanding where different groups agree and disagree can help them better serve the public interest.
John Kotcher receives funding from The U.S. Energy Foundation, The Kresge Foundation, and The Commonwealth Fund.
Teresa Myers receives funding from the U.S. Energy Foundation.

articles.title: Murder of Black suffrage leader Octavius Catto reveals why Election Day 1871 was one of the most violent in Philadelphia history
articles.author: Timothy Welbeck, Director of the Center for Anti-Racism, Temple University
paras: Octavius Valentine Catto died as he lived, advocating for a more equitable society. Accordingly, the city of Philadelphia has decided to honor his legacy – again.
Philadelphia previously honored Catto with a commemorative statue outside City Hall in 2017. Of the city’s 1,500 public statues, it was the first to honor an individual Black person.
On Oct. 8, 2026, the intersection of 8th and South streets was formally renamed Octavius Catto Way. This is where Catto was assassinated 155 years ago during a tumultuous Election Day in 1871.
Speaking at the renaming ceremony, NAACP Philadelphia Branch President Catherine Hicks said the moment was about ensuring Catto’s legacy was remembered and understood.

As a civil rights lawyer and professor in the Africology and African American Studies department at Temple University, I find Catto’s activism immensely important. I hope more Philadelphians are encouraged to learn about Octavius Catto, the man former Philadelphia Mayor Jim Kenney described as the “Jackie Robinson and Rosa Parks of his day.”
A teacher, baseball player and civil rights leader

Octavius Catto was born in Charleston, South Carolina, in 1839 to a free Black woman named Sarah Isabella Cain and a formerly enslaved man named William Catto, who purchased his freedom and later became a Presbyterian minister.

William Catto brought his family north to Baltimore with plans to eventually travel to Liberia as missionaries. William Catto had to adjust his plans when members of Charleston’s Presbyterian leadership discovered a letter he had written they believed would incite an insurrection among enslaved people. They alleged the letter would “excite discontent and insurrection among the slaves.” An arrest warrant was issued for William and Sarah. They fled Baltimore and later settled in Philadelphia. There, William Catto would become an abolitionist, which had a profound influence on his son Octavius.

Octavius Catto spent his formative years and subsequently launched his career as a public servant in Philadelphia. He attended the Institute for Colored Youth – now Cheyney University – and graduated at the top of his class in 1858.

The next year, he started teaching English and mathematics at the institute. By his early 30s, Catto had worked with Frederick Douglass to recruit all-Black regiments to fight for the Union Army during the Civil War. He co-founded, managed and played for an all-Black baseball team, the Philadelphian Pythians baseball club. He also worked with other civil rights leaders like Lucretia Mott and his fiancé, Caroline LeCount, to desegregate Philadelphia’s horse-drawn streetcars and the Franklin Institute.
The fight for Black suffrage in Philadelphia

More than a century before the civil rights protests erupted in Selma and Birmingham, Octavius Catto led desegregation efforts and voting rights campaigns in Philadelphia in the 1860s. The New York Times covered some of his desegregation efforts in 1867.

His civil rights advocacy was met with violent opposition, especially after the ratification of the 15th Amendment in February of 1870. The 15th Amendment guaranteed voting rights for citizens regardless of their “race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” Legal scholars such as Travis Crum argue the 15th Amendment “re-founded the United States as a multiracial democracy.” It gave the federal government key enforcement powers that prior legislative acts that secured the right to vote – such as the First Reconstruction Act – did not have.

In 1780, nine decades before Catto’s murder, the Pennsylvania General Assembly had passed the Act of Gradual Abolition of Slavery, which set the conditions freeing Pennsylvania’s enslaved people. It was the first legislation of its kind in America.

Despite these provisions, varying interpretations of Pennsylvania’s Constitution of 1776 left it unclear whether Black men could vote without restriction. The state Constitution restricted the vote to freemen, which it defined as “of full age of twenty-one years, having resided in this State for one whole year before the day of election … and paid public taxes during that time.”
Sixty-two years later, the state made it painfully clear who it intended to allow to vote. In 1838, Pennsylvania’s Constitution explicitly restricted the right to vote to “white freemen.”

Philadelphia became a key location for the fight for suffrage and other pivotal civil rights. The city had a large Black population, a storied history of abolition and an abundance of Black institutions, yet racial discrimination was still endemic.
Targeted by white supremacists

Election Day of 1871 was one of the most consequential in the history of Philadelphia, at the time an epicenter for the simmering tensions surrounding Black suffrage. According to W.E.B. Du Bois’ “The Philadelphia Negro,” about 5,500 Black men were eligible to vote in 1870. The prospect of Black men voting in the election sparked violent outrage in the city.
Both city officials and private citizens engaged in targeted violence to intimidate Black voters. Armed mobs harassed Black neighborhoods, attacked residents and forcibly closed polling locations.

Four Black Philadelphians – Levi Bolden, Isaac Chase, Jacob Gordon and Moses Wright – died during the coordinated racial violence that occurred that day and the evening before. It all left many of the city’s Black residents “considerably frightened,” according to a Philadelphia Inquirer report. Catto became a fifth victim.
Around 3:30 p.m., Catto was standing near his Philadelphia home when Frank Kelly, a political operative who opposed Black suffrage, fatally shot him.

Catto’s impassioned advocacy had made him a target of white supremacists in the region, but he did not waver in the face of this growing danger. In speaking of Catto’s legacy, Du Bois wrote, “And so closed the career of a man of splendid equipment, rare force of character, whose life was so interwoven with all that was good about us, as to make it stand out in bold relief, as a pattern for those who have followed after.”
Dedicated to empowering Black Philadelphians

Philadelphia Martyrs Day is an annual observance that pays homage to the five Philadelphia men who fought for Black suffrage and were killed in the 1871 election. These memorials often emphasize Catto because of his civil rights and voting rights advocacy.

Despite this and the statue outside City Hall, I and others in Philadelphia believe Catto’s influence remains largely unsung. In describing the importance of the street renaming, Leland Morroccos, executive director of It’s the Little Things Foundation, a local civic engagement and community advocacy organization, said, “Octavius Valentine Catto deserves to be remembered not simply as a name in Philadelphia’s history, but as a man who devoted his life to educating, organizing and empowering Black Philadelphians to participate fully in the civic life of their city and their country.”
“Philadelphia should forever remember Octavius V. Catto,” Morroccos continued, “not only for how he died, but for how he lived, what he believed, and the doors he worked to open for others.”
I hope all who stroll along Octavius Catto Way will come to learn that too.

articles.title: Why the Paramount-Warner merger is a problem for democracy
articles.author: Seth Ashley, Associate Professor of Journalism and Media Communication, Colorado State University
paras: Media critic Ben Bagdikian warned in 2004 that five corporations had accumulated “more communications power than was exercised by any despot or dictatorship in history.” More than 20 years later, a major media merger is bringing his warning back into focus.

Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in October 2026 created a new company, Skydance Corporation. It now owns CNN and CBS News, Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, HBO and Paramount+, along with a sprawling collection of cable networks, live sports and entertainment franchises. The deal is valued at about US$110 billion including debt, and Skydance expects to cut at least $6 billion in costs within three years.

A coalition of 12 states sued to stop the merger on antitrust grounds, arguing that it would reduce competition in movies and television. The eventual settlement required a multiyear movie production and theatrical release guarantee and an editorial independence board for CNN and CBS News. CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss remain in charge, but both ultimately report to Skydance CEO David Ellison.

Lawmakers have already raised concerns about possible political influence over CBS News, though Ellison has denied interfering with coverage. President Donald Trump, a frequent CNN critic, publicly praised the merger.

As a scholar who studies the role of media in democratic societies, I believe that size and ownership matter. Whoever owns the media chooses its leaders, approves its budgets and decides where to cut $6 billion. The same market pressures pushing media companies toward greater scale and efficiency can undermine the independent reporting and diversity of voices that democracy depends on.
When media are more than ordinary products
Since broadcasting began, American media policy has wrestled with how to support the information needs of a democracy.

As my work on the origins of media systems shows, the United States built a largely private, commercial broadcasting system while Britain created the publicly funded BBC. Behind those choices were different ideas about whether broadcasting should operate primarily as a business or carry broader obligations to the public.

The market view became increasingly dominant in the U.S. In 1981, the Ronald Reagan-era chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, Mark Fowler, famously described television as “a toaster with pictures.” He argued that broadcasters should largely respond to audiences through ordinary market forces.

But as media scholar Robert McChesney argued in 1999, concentrated commercial media had become a “significant antidemocratic force.” What makes money for a media company and what citizens need from a media system are not always the same thing.
We’ve seen this film before.

Local television stations acquired by Sinclair Broadcast Group in 2017 shifted coverage away from local politics and toward national political stories. As research shows, communities that lose local media coverage can see less competition and participation in elections.
Mergers, however, make sense in the logic of the market. Warner and Paramount must compete with Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, Apple and other companies with enormous resources and global reach.

But having fewer competitors can also mean there’s less pressure to improve quality or hold down prices. And the efficiencies of media consolidation often come from producing less original content with fewer people.
Concerns about media power are hardly new.

The 1947 Hutchins Commission on Freedom of the Press warned about control of mass communication becoming concentrated in fewer hands, and it encouraged greater social responsibility. For decades, the FCC placed limits on broadcast ownership to support competition and diversity.

Digital media seemed to blow open the gates that limited participation, but a new class of gatekeepers arrived. While Bagdikian mainly worried about companies that owned newspapers, TV networks and movie studios, today’s media power lies in the hands of platforms, streamers and tech giants.

Social and video platforms have overtaken TV and news sites as the most common way people access news in dozens of countries studied in 2026 by the Reuters Institute. News organizations may still produce a story, but Google, YouTube, Facebook, TikTok and artificial intelligence can determine whether anyone sees it.
For social platforms, attention is the commodity. Likes, shares, comments, clicks and watch time help determine what gets promoted. And more time on the platform means more opportunities to sell ads.

It’s now well documented that social media feeds ranked for that kind of engagement expose people to more toxic political content and moral outrage than chronological feeds. They also increase perceptions of hostility between political groups.
Americans certainly consume enough media, with combined use at more than 13 hours a day.

Yet Americans do not seem especially well-informed or confident about the information they receive. Only 33% say they trust mass media to report the news fully and fairly, compared with 68% when Gallup first asked in 1972, and about half say they have difficulty determining what is true in the news. More than a third cannot name all three branches of the federal government.
Media concentration did not cause all of these problems. But decades of greater media abundance have not solved problems of knowledge, misinformation or trust.
Who produces the information democracy needs?
Democracy assumes that citizens will have enough information to make choices and hold powerful institutions accountable. But markets provide no guarantee that anyone will produce it.

As media scholar C. Edwin Baker explained in 2009, journalism creates benefits that extend far beyond the person who buys a newspaper or subscription. A monthslong investigation of corruption might benefit an entire city, including thousands of people who never pay for the reporting. But the media organization still has to cover the cost.
That’s why restoring journalism requires public and nonprofit alternatives to combat market failures, as media scholar Victor Pickard has laid out.

Other democracies already rely more heavily on a mix of commercial and public media. Research in 2009 comparing the U.S. with Britain, Denmark and Finland found that stronger public service outlets carried more public affairs and international news and were associated with greater political knowledge.

This doesn’t have to be a partisan issue. Regardless of who is in power, citizens benefit from vibrant journalism with the resources and independence to investigate government, business and other powerful institutions.

Media literacy can help citizens understand why the system works this way. As I argue in my 2019 book, News Literacy and Democracy, examining media means understanding the structures and institutions behind it – who owns them, how they make money and what pressures shape what gets produced.
But there are limits to what we can ask individual news consumers to fix.

People can learn to check sources and spot misinformation, but they can’t change market forces. The Paramount-Warner merger makes sense according to the logic of the market, and I believe that’s the problem. The same pressures that push media companies toward greater scale and lower costs can work against creating the media environment that democracy needs to thrive.

articles.title: Inside two prison systems: why Denmark and the UK punish so differently
articles.author: Julie Laursen, Associate professor in Criminology, University of Copenhagen
paras: It has been said that a society should be judged not by how it treats its outstanding citizens but by how it treats people who break the law.
I research prisons and am interested in what incarceration reveals about the relationship between the state and the people in its care.

By this standard, the UK and Denmark tell very different stories. In 2025, Denmark’s prison population stood at around 69 people per 100,000 residents, compared with about 170 per 100,000 in the UK – roughly two and a half times higher.

One way to understand this difference is through welfare. With its wide range of universal welfare state services such as heavily subsidised daycare, free healthcare, free education and high standards of public services, Denmark’s criminal justice system has traditionally placed greater emphasis on rehabilitation and reintegration. Prisoners retain the right to vote, maintain closer contact with family and are generally encouraged to participate in ordinary social life where possible.

Health Gap / Sundhedskløften is a collaborative series from The Conversation UK and Denmark’s Videnskab.dk exploring what the two countries can learn from each other when it comes to health and wellbeing.

From cycling and alcohol to inequality, healthcare and everyday habits, the series looks beyond hospitals and medical treatment to explore how culture, politics and society shape the way people live – and how healthy they are.

The UK, while still a welfare state, is more uneven in its provision. And these social differences are reflected in criminal justice policy. This results in higher incarceration rates in the UK, as well as more challenging prison conditions and a stronger emphasis on punishment and deterrence.

Indeed, my previous research, comparing prisons in England and Wales with another Nordic country, Norway, found that imprisonment in the UK is often experienced as unpredictable and austere. Norway’s system, meanwhile – which is closer to the Danish system – felt more structured and respectful.

Yet this difference in approach is only relatively recent. After the second world war, both countries used open prisons widely, spearheaded humane and progressive politics and had low imprisonment rates.

From the 1980s onwards, however, the UK increasingly moved towards a more punitive approach to criminal justice. Under Margaret Thatcher’s government and subsequent administrations, prison populations grew substantially while conditions in many prisons deteriorated.
The question is: which works best? Tough on crime policies that dramatically increase the prison population, or welfare-based decision making with an emphasis on rehabilitation?

On the surface, the outcomes can look surprisingly similar. Around 30% of prisoners released in Denmark go on to reoffend, compared with 29% in England and Wales. But that comparison changes when you look more closely.
For those serving short sentences of under a year, reoffending is around 34% in Denmark. Whereas this figure almost doubles for the UK, with roughly 66% of prisoners going on to reoffend.

The disruption caused by short-term imprisonment – loss of housing, employment, relationships and social stability – is particularly severe in the UK, where prisoners often leave custody with limited support.
Yet Denmark should not be romanticised. Danish prisons may be safer, more humane and more “survivable” than many prisons in the UK, but they also contain notable problems.
In Denmark, prisons have faced criticism over the use of pre-trial isolation, lack of care for women in custody, and the treatment of gang-affiliated prisoners.

In January 2026, the death of a prisoner in North Jutland triggered large protests from prisoners and their families – amid concerns that serious health issues were not properly addressed. The prisoner was reportedly experiencing intense abdominal and stomach pain in the days leading up to this death. With claims from inmates that he repeatedly sought medical attention before dying in his cell.
Denmark’s prison service has also lost around 30% of its staff over the past decade, with prisons running at or above capacity.

The UK system has faced similar problems in recent years. Around 3,000 prison officers leave their roles every year in England and Wales, contributing to a constant cycle of recruitment and turnover. Combined with overcrowding, lack of rehabilitative initiatives and rising violence, it leaves many prisons stretched thin.

These pressures are reshaping daily life inside. In Denmark, open prisons – once seen as central to the rehabilitative approach – are changing. Increasingly, low-risk prisoners serve their sentences in the community under electronic tag, meaning open prisons now tend to be filled with more vulnerable and complex cases.
Drugs can be an issue. Staff are also often young and still training, meaning that maintaining order can be a challenge.

In both countries, high-security prisoners can spend up to 22 hours a day in their cells due to staff shortages and restricted regimes. It’s a reminder that very different systems can produce similarly harsh conditions under pressure.

Bjørn*, a prisoner I spoke with during my fieldwork in a high-security prison in Denmark, was often transferred between prisons where he was kept in strict conditions because he was considered a “difficult” prisoner.

Reflecting on his previous sentence, he said: “I was angry with the authorities when I went in. When I got out, I hated them”. His experience illustrates how punishment that relies heavily on containment can create prisons that are more volatile for both staff and prisoners.
But as my research also found, in Denmark, imprisonment is often seen in more conditional terms.

As, Noah* – another of of the prisoners I spoke with – put it, it’s almost like a “contract” between the individual and the state, where efforts to change are meant to be met with a real chance of release. In other words, Danes have high expectations of their state, even when it punishes them.
That reflects the wider level of trust in public institutions found in Denmark: around 60% of Danes say they trust their government, compared with about 33% in the UK.
In England and Wales, prisoners and staff alike describe a system shaped by overcrowding, staff shortages and instability, with fewer opportunities for rehabilitation.
In this sense, the comparison between Denmark and the UK is not a straightforward story of “humane” versus “punitive” systems. But something more complicated about trust, expectations and pressure.

That said, the Danish Government has recently launched a new strategy for punishment with longer sentences alongside more rehabilitative initiatives. These proposals have been met with concern as to whether a more rehabilitative model can survive when resources are stretched.

In the end, though, the differences between Denmark and the UK are not fixed. Because prison systems are not just shaped by national philosophies on punishment, but also by the political choices that determine whether rehabilitation is adequately funded and supported.
*Prisoners’ names have been changed
This series was commissioned as part of a partnership between Videnskab.dk and The Conversation, where articles are published in English and Danish.
Julie Laursen receives funding from Independent Research Fund Denmark.

articles.title: Are the UK authorities letting down survivors of modern slavery?
articles.author: Marija Jovanovic, Research Fellow in Business and Human Rights, Bonavero Institute of Human Rights, University of Oxford
paras: The adoption of the Slavery Convention 100 years ago was a landmark moment for the international prohibition of slavery. It also laid foundations for human rights movements across the world.

The United Kingdom played an important role in the global abolitionist movement and the development of human rights law. The centenary of the convention was therefore an opportunity to assess how effectively it is meeting those commitments today.
International anti-trafficking law requires states to prevent and combat human trafficking, protect victims and their human rights and cooperate with other states.

The term “modern slavery” is used to describe severe exploitation including human trafficking, forced labour, servitude and slavery. It is the product of multiple systems that can both prevent exploitation and, at the same time, create the conditions for it. It cannot be tackled effectively if the policies governing immigration, employment, business and criminal justice are considered separately.

Immigration rules can create, intensify, or mitigate someone’s vulnerability to exploitation. Labour market regulation can either prevent poor working conditions from escalating into forced labour or allow exploitation to become entrenched.
Criminal justice determines both how we hold exploiters accountable and how we treat people who commit offences as a result of exploitation.
These systems are governed separately, whilst people experiencing severe exploitation encounter issues simultaneously.

Labour exploitation illustrates this. It accounted for 45% of all adult cases of modern slavery referred to the national referral mechanism in 2025. More than nine in ten of these people were migrant workers. This points to challenges beyond those that the Modern Slavery Act 2015, a centrepiece of the UK’s laws in this area, is currently addressing.

If migrant workers are disproportionately represented among those experiencing labour exploitation, we must ask how the immigration and labour market rules governing their recruitment and employment themselves create or exacerbate vulnerability.

Social care provides an example. International workers have been recruited to meet serious workforce shortages, yet the government has acknowledged large-scale non-compliance and exploitation in the sector.

Workers recognised as modern slavery victims will soon be able to change employer rather than remain tied to an exploiting sponsor. But that protection comes after a survivor is identified. More action is needed before exploitation becomes sufficiently severe to be labelled modern slavery.
The UK has relied heavily on requiring companies to report what they are doing about modern slavery in their supply chains.

Reporting alone is not enough, and the UK is falling behind other countries when it comes to regulating company activities. This risks this country becoming a “dumping ground” for goods produced with forced labour.
When one policy undermines another
Immigration enforcement and victim protection provide perhaps the clearest examples of policies working against each other.

Human rights law requires states to identify potential victims irrespective of the victim’s conduct. Yet the recently introduced immigration and asylum bill requires delayed disclosure, omissions, and inconsistencies to count against a person’s credibility when making a claim about exploitation. Claims made by adults facing removal from the UK must be treated as made in bad faith, excluding them from protection.

These measures shift responsibility for identification from the state onto individual victims, despite knowledge that people most in need of protection may be least able to recognise themselves as victims. They struggle to disclose exploitation promptly, or provide a complete and consistent account of their experience. Failure to identify victims also allows exploiters to escape investigation and punishment.

The bill also removes recovery from physical or psychological harm caused by the exploitation as a basis for temporary leave to remain, despite recovery and protection being a precondition for a person’s decision to engage with law enforcement. This in turn risks weakening already low rates of prosecution.

For people experiencing exploitation, these are not abstract issues. They determine whether someone is recognised and supported, can leave an exploitative job, or feels able to approach authorities without risking detention or removal.
A ‘whole-systems’ response needs evidence

A coherent response requires data, yet basic gaps remain in what we know about modern slavery in the UK. We lack data on labour exploitation by sector and occupation, repeat referrals, limiting understanding of re-trafficking, compensation received by survivors, or the prevalence of survivors within custodial settings in the UK.

Most significantly, there is a glaring evidence gap around claims that the referral system is being abused. In 2025, 23,411 potential victims were referred, yet of 224 confirmed disqualifications, only six were on grounds of bad faith. Without robust evidence, we cannot know whether policies prevent exploitation, displace it elsewhere, or increase vulnerability.

One hundred years after the Slavery Convention, the UK has many of the tools needed to tackle modern slavery, but they are not working in sync. Today’s key challenge is to build a coherent “whole-systems” approach underpinned by robust evidence and informed by lived experience. Immigration, labour regulation, business accountability, victim protection, and criminal justice must reinforce rather than undermine each other.
Marija Jovanovic receives funding from The Arts and Humanities Research Council and The Sigrid Rausing Trust.

articles.title: More than 119 million Brazilians voted in the Oct. 4 election – including about 21,000 Florida residents
articles.author: Rafael R. Ioris, Professor of Modern Latin America History, University of Denver
paras: More than 119 million Brazilians voted on Oct. 4, 2026, in the national elections to select the country’s next president and the governors of all 27 states, among other government officials.
That’s nearly 75% of the approximately 159 million eligible voters. Unlike in the U.S., voting is mandatory in Brazil for all citizens between the ages of 18 and 70.
This includes nearly 1 million Brazilians who currently live outside the country. About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in Boston, New York and Miami.

Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro, managed to get over 50% of the votes, Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election.

Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy. But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system. As a scholar of Latin American history and politics, and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest.

Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online. In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population. Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up 15 polling places in 12 states. Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters.

Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours. Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing.
So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4.

It’s unclear whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though some Brazilians say they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots. Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that if their immigration status was precarious, they should not vote.

What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations. If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to resist overt pressures from Washington to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China.

On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have much closer relations with the U.S. That is why President Donald Trump would prefer to have a Bolsonaro in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated.

Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities. But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the largest numbers of Brazilian residents. This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America.

In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula. This seems to be another indication of the polarization that has shaped this key election and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years.
I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum for some time.

Even though Lula managed to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Bolsonarismo – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained the most influential political force in the country. This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s.

Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections, it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today.
A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to becoming a mature democracy, after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates.
But now, considering the lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement, this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election.

Rafael R. Ioris does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Democrats distance themselves from trans rights – close midterm races may show whether that pays off
articles.author: Dorian Rhea Debussy, Lecturer of Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, The Ohio State University
paras: A wave of anti-transgender legislation has appeared in statehouses across the country over the past few years. Now, transgender issues are a recurring topic on the 2026 midterm campaign trail.

As a scholar of LGBTQ+ politics and history, I’ve noticed surprising trends in how Democrats in key states like Texas and Ohio talk about policies focused on transgender people, as the party vies for control of Congress.

With a rise in anti-trans rhetoric from the White House, some Democrats are using similar messaging in an attempt to secure undecided voters. In my assessment, this approach could alienate moderates, progressives and LGBTQ+ people more broadly.
Democratic candidates have split sharply on transition-related care and inclusion in school sports.

In Massachusetts, Rep. Seth Moulton came out against transgender girls competing in school sports, just days after President Donald Trump’s victory in November 2024. But Sen. Ed Markey, Moulton’s primary opponent for the Senate seat, took the opposite approach, stating his unwavering support for transgender rights.

Markey polled ahead of Moulton throughout 2026 and won the primary by nearly 30 percentage points. Public opinion data shows that two-thirds of Democratic likely primary voters in Massachusetts said they would be less likely to back a candidate who opposes transgender rights.

Other Democrats, especially in Southern and Midwestern states, are taking a more conservative approach to transgender rights. In Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has reversed his past support for transgender athletes.

Months after his March primary victory against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, Talarico said in a Fox News interview that he would “oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”
According to scholars and media watchdog groups like GLAAD, appeals to “safety” and “fairness” are common anti-trans dog whistles that perpetuate misinformation about transgender athletes.

The shift has not resulted in a polling bump for Talarico in his race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Polls of likely voters from July to early September gave Talarico an average lead of 3.16 percentage points. Polls since mid-September put his average lead at 2.66 percentage points.

Republican-aligned super PACs are also emphasizing transgender issues. Elon Musk’s America PAC has spent US$100 million on anti-trans ads in battleground states like Texas, Ohio and Alaska. Some of these ads feature people implied to be transgender women, though it is unclear whether they were actors or AI-generated.
With the prevalence of anti-trans ads, Democratic campaigns are responding in different ways. Some are veering to the right by mirroring GOP positions, like transgender exclusion from school sports.

Ohio offers clear examples of this gamble. In June, the state’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, made an anti-trans comment, referring to transgender girls as “boys.” This quickly drew criticism from statewide LGBTQ+ groups and community leaders.

In Ohio’s 9th congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur’s campaign has run multiple anti-trans ads focusing on parental rights and transgender children in school sports, saying that the congresswoman voted to keep “transgender ideology” out of schools. The campaign also recently ran mailers with this message.

Kaptur’s county party condemned the ads, saying they were “disappointed and ashamed” of her campaign. When the state party’s Pride Caucus shared the county party’s statement on social media, the post was deleted. Pride Caucus members accused state party leadership of censorship; weeks later, transgender leaders from the caucus resigned in protest.

In contrast, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, has focused his campaign ads on affordability, data center regulations and the Epstein files without wavering on his support for transgender rights, as Acton and Kaptur have.
After a misleading super PAC ad about transgender healthcare from the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund, Brown’s campaign released a counter ad correcting the claim before pivoting to affordability.

Days later, the same GOP super PAC released another ad targeting Brown. Reporting has confirmed that the ad, which features an adult from Texas rather than Ohio, is factually inaccurate and misleading.

Recent polling suggests Brown is outperforming his fellow Democrat Acton, who is running for governor, by 2 percentage points. While these polls don’t isolate the effect of a single issue, Acton has faced criticism from the public, in addition to state and national LGBTQ+ organizations.

Amid rising prices on fuel and food, upticks in unemployment and a national hiring slowdown, consumer confidence in the economy has dropped to its lowest point in over a decade. Nationally, many Democrats are trying to emphasize these points. To counter that message, some Republicans continue to emphasize “culture war” issues like transgender rights.

Currently, Democrats outperform Republicans on the generic congressional ballot – a polling tool that asks voters which party they’d back without naming candidates. But messaging on transgender rights may be a tipping point for midterm voters.

As a growing electorate of 12% of the U.S. adult population and with a voter turnout rate of roughly 80%, LGBTQ+ people are a strong voting bloc. Recent polling indicates that two-thirds of LGBTQ+ adults said they would be extremely to somewhat comfortable with trans athletes competing on sports teams that don’t match their sex at birth.

In battleground states, anti-trans messages could cost votes and spell defeat for Democrats who rely on them. The risk is especially high in states like Ohio and Texas, where races are close and LGBTQ+ adults are estimated to make up more than 11% of the adult population.

In Texas, Talarico’s lead could be undone by depressed turnout among the Lone Star State’s 2.24 million LGBTQ+ adults. In Ohio, home to roughly 883,000 LGBTQ+ adults, Acton’s gubernatorial race and Kaptur’s congressional district race are both statistical ties.
With control of Congress up for grabs, campaign messaging missteps could have national implications.

articles.title: Unpicking the pensions triple lock: where it came from, and what might happen next
articles.author: Maria Evandrou, Professor of Gerontology, University of Southampton
paras: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made the politically risky decision to adjust the pensions triple lock from April 2030.

Speaking at this year’s Labour Party Conference, he said: “Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen.”
But what is the triple lock, and why was the announcement so controversial?

The triple lock is a mechanism that provides a guaranteed increase in the basic and new state pension. It raises it by whichever is highest among average earnings growth, price inflation, or 2.5% and ensures that state pension payments increase in value every April.

Politicians have long considered any challenge to the triple lock to be highly risky to their chances at the ballot box. But how long has the mechanism been in place and what were the reasons for its introduction?

Increasing the value of pensions has been hotly debated since the early 1970s. Back then, the Labour government introduced legislation to increase long-term benefits and state pensions in line with earnings or prices, whichever was higher – a “double lock” on pensions growth.

But by the late 1970s, the governing Conservative party deemed this mechanism “unsustainable” because of the same “ratchet effect” that the triple lock is now criticised for. In other words, for the rest of the population, their wages grew in response to inflation – but pensioners enjoyed the rise every year. Pensions were then linked to prices only, rather than slower-growing earnings.

During the 1980s and 1990s, concerns grew about a growing number of people falling into poverty in later life. Consecutive governments debated whether the link to earnings should be restored. At the same time, pensioners were experiencing a steady decrease in the value of the state pension relative to average earnings. This went from a peak of 26% of average earnings in 1979 to around 16% of average earnings between 2000 and 2010.

In 1999, there was a reckoning when pensioners received an increase of just 75p per week after a period of low inflation. The tiny uptick sparked anger and then-chancellor Gordon Brown was under pressure to act. Finally, in 2002, the Labour government legislated to increase pensions by the higher of 2.5% or price inflation. The double lock was back in place.

A key point came when the (first) Pensions Commission in 2005 published its recommendation that the government restore the link of pensions with earnings. This was a bid to reduce the risk of pensioners falling into poverty and placing pressure on the system of means-tested benefits.

This recommendation was followed by the announcement of a triple lock by the Conservative/Liberal Democrat coalition government in its first budget in 2010. It had been a key promise in the Lib Dem manifesto, and it was implemented in 2011 by then-chancellor George Osborne.

Since 2011, the triple lock has increased the value of the state pension considerably. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) showed that between 2010-2023, the median disposable household income for pensioners rose by 15%. Cross-party support for maintaining the triple lock during the 2019 general election demonstrated a broad commitment to the steady increase of the state pension.

However, while average incomes in later life have risen, the gap between poorer pensioners and those on average incomes has widened. Relative poverty among pensioners rose from 13% in 2011, to 16% in 2022. Thus, the triple lock has not necessarily meant that fewer? pensioners are living in poverty.

At the same time, the key safety net for low-income pensioners is not the state pension alone. Historically, this was provided by something called the minimum income guarantee. This is a means-tested benefit which ensures that pensioners’ weekly income does not fall below a legally set minimum (£238 per week for a single person in 2026/7, and £363.25 for a couple), which was also linked to earnings.

The minimum income guarantee was replaced by the guarantee element of pension credit (a means-tested benefit that tops up the income of poorer pensioners). This move towards some kind of guarantee of a minimum income didn’t come with the fanfare of the triple lock – but it did make a big difference to pensioners’ incomes before the triple lock was introduced.

The Resolution Foundation, an independent thinktank focused on raising UK living standards, estimated that there was a 15.8 percentage point fall in pensioner relative poverty between 1997-98 and 2011-12, as growing incomes for poor pensioners closed the gap with the non-pensioner median income.
But there are still an estimated 760,000 vulnerable pensioners who are eligible for means-tested pension credit, but who failed to claim it in 2025/6.

The government’s own analysis shows that this happens for a number of reasons: people may not have heard of it, or don’t know who to contact in order to claim it. The application process is complicated, and for some there may be stigma attached to claiming.

One solution to lifting more pensioners out of poverty might be increasing the value of pension credit and improving its take-up. It is notable that the triple lock does not apply to pension credit or to winter fuel payments, which use different criteria to work out the rate of increase.

Analysis by the IFS illustrates that the “new” triple lock, as outlined in Burnham’s speech, is still expected to generate an increase in the value of the state pension in the future. However, such increase will not permanently “ratchet up” the level of the state pension in the same way as the “old” triple lock.

articles.title: When abortion and surrogacy law collide, contracts can’t answer the hardest questions
articles.author: Sonia Suter, Professor of Law, George Washington University
paras: Surrogacy arrangements – agreements for someone to carry a pregnancy for the intended parents – have existed for millennia, and modern surrogacy contracts for half a century.

These contracts typically address parental rights, the possibility of abortion, medical instructions, health insurance and payment of expenses, each side with its own legal representation. The contracts are usually honored, resulting in thousands of babies born through surrogacy in the U.S., at a cost that can top US$200,000 when agencies are involved.

In a 2026 case, surrogate McKenna West refused the intended parents’ request for an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart condition. The case raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the surrogate’s bodily autonomy collides with the intended parents’ wishes?

As scholars of reproductive justice and family law, we see this case as an example of how rapidly changing abortion laws, reproductive technology and family law can create conflicts that surrogacy contracts cannot necessarily anticipate.

West’s contract stated that “there shall be a termination of the pregnancy for a fetal abnormality … if the Intended Parents request” it. She later wrote that “their lawyer and my own former lawyer sent me letters threatening six-figure penalties if I didn’t comply with their demand to terminate.”

Instead, West moved from Alaska to Texas, where she had family support and believed the baby, when born, could get needed care. Moreover, she knew that Texas bans abortion in almost all circumstances. Meanwhile, the intended parents, who lived in California, obtained a court order before the birth stating they would become the legal parents once the baby was born.

Before West gave birth, the Texas attorney general obtained a court order requiring lifesaving care for the baby, stating that “the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the lifesaving surgery.” West sought custody but was willing to drop her claims if the couple agreed to the baby’s treatment.

After the Texas courts upheld the intended parents’ rights, West asked the Supreme Court to intervene so she could receive “further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” The court declined, leaving West no rights to the baby.

In a similar 2012 case, surrogate Crystal Kelley signed a contract allowing the intended parents to call for an abortion in case of a severe fetal abnormality. When the fetus was diagnosed with a heart defect and other serious anomalies, the parents asked Kelley to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and left Connecticut, where she would not have had parental rights, for Michigan, which at the time would treat her as the legal mother. Kelley placed the baby for adoption, and the girl’s adoptive parents raised her until her death at 8.

In the 1988 Baby M case, a surrogate who was also the genetic mother insisted she should be the mother despite signing a contract to relinquish parental rights. The New Jersey Supreme Court voided that contract because it held that she could not give up her parental rights before birth. As a result, it recognized the surrogate as the legal mother but awarded custody to the father. She later received visitation rights.
A state-by-state patchwork
Surrogacy contracts establishing legal parentage are enforceable in a number of states. But surrogacy laws vary by state, creating a patchwork with respect to enforceability.

West’s journey, for example, involved three states – Alaska, Texas and the intended parents’ state of California. They are deemed surrogacy-friendly, meaning contracts are relatively easy to enforce there, though the states diverge sharply on abortion.

Surrogacy agreements may require the surrogate to restrict travel, eat nutritiously and cooperate with healthcare providers. As in the West and Kelley cases, agreements may also specify when the surrogate could be asked to abort or, if pregnant with multiple fetuses, selectively terminate.
These abortion provisions have rarely been tested in court, and West’s case hasn’t resolved whether they are enforceable. Rather, they raise the question: Can anyone be forced to have an abortion?

After the Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which held there is no fundamental right to abortion, states have determined their own abortion laws. In states like Texas, abortion provisions in surrogacy contracts are unenforceable. But even where abortion is legal, a court would likely refuse to compel an abortion, given the surrogate’s bodily autonomy.
A surrogate’s control over her body may be more limited, however, when intended parents seek to enforce provisions meant to protect the fetus.

If a physician recommends a C-section for the fetus’s well-being and the surrogate refuses, for example, a court might enforce a contract clause requiring her “to cooperate with her medical providers.”
Even before 2022, when abortion was still a federal constitutional right, courts in some – but not all – jurisdictions ordered C-sections against the pregnant person’s wishes.
In other words, bodily autonomy has never been absolute for pregnant people.
Since Dobbs, surrogacy and abortion have become increasingly intertwined.

In 2025, a Florida judge questioned the constitutionality of surrogacy on fetal-personhood grounds – the legal theory that an unborn fetus or embryo has the same legal rights as a born human – even as he granted the intended parents parental rights.

In his view, there can be no “contractual ownership interest over the unborn baby.” Florida’s attorney general took the argument further, declaring that the couple’s contract with the surrogate violated the 13th Amendment’s ban on slavery. A spokesperson said he was concerned “about any case where a surrogacy company profits off the sale of children.”

Some conservative legislators and advocacy groups have also been challenging the legitimacy of surrogacy, a few with plans to limit or even ban it. Consequently, in states that take fetal and embryo personhood seriously, surrogacy contracts and even IVF could become unavailable.

West’s case has surfaced starkly different views of what is at stake. For some, surrogacy is a form of baby selling that should not be allowed. For others, it is a way for intended parents to create families and for surrogates to support them.

Surrogacy asks the law to recognize both the interests of people who intend to become parents and the autonomy of the person who is pregnant. Dobbs has made that balance harder to maintain by inviting fetal-personhood principles into areas of law that had not previously treated fetuses or embryos as persons.

articles.title: The oil market that sets today’s gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
articles.author: Brian C. Black, Distinguished Professor of History and Environmental Studies, Penn State
paras: The fall of 2026 is a moment of energy centrality, when geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans’ everyday lives.
In Pennsylvania, the statewide diesel price averages US$6.50 per gallon. In Iowa, farmers are paying more than $6 a gallon for diesel. And in Alaska, unleaded gas runs more than $9 a gallon.

As a distinguished professor of history and environmental studies at Penn State Altoona, I write widely about oil and energy issues. This moment has me thinking about how the oil industry began nearly 170 years ago in northwestern Pennsylvania.
Setting crude prices in Oil City

In 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil along Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. His well was funded by investors from New Bedford, Massachusetts, who were looking for a replacement for whale oil, which was expensive and challenging to acquire.

The first oil deals were struck on the streets of Oil City, about 90 miles north of Pittsburgh, while traders were still working out basic questions about “rock oil,” as crude was then called: What was it good for, and how much should it cost?

To create a more formal system, the oil traders developed a railroad car designed to be a rolling oil exchange on the Oil Creek Railway. It made 13 stops daily between Titusville and Oil City, and trading was conducted on the honor system, with no written certificates of purchase or sale.
As the industry quickly grew, an oil exchange office was set up in the Arlington Hotel in Oil City.

Traders pushed for a building of their own, arguing that a growing industry needed a more formal market. By 1874, Pennsylvania’s Oil Valley was producing roughly 30,000 barrels of crude oil a day, which sold for an average of about $1.15 a barrel.

Rather than physically moving barrels around, trading had moved from handshakes to paper. Pipelines issued certificates representing the oil in their lines. Traders bought and sold the paper certificates representing oil, often trading the same barrels many times in a single day. As a result, the volume of oil changing hands could reach 10 million to 14 million barrels a day, hundreds of times more than the wells actually produced.
In April 1874, a group of Oil City oil men received a state charter to form the Oil City Oil Exchange. Construction started in July 1877 at the corner of Center and Seneca streets.

When the Oil Exchange opened in April 1878, the local newspaper called it “the largest and most elaborate structure ever erected in the Oil Region.” The building, the paper said, reflected how big the speculative side of the oil trade had become. Standard Oil, the nation’s largest oil company at the time, owned by John D. Rockefeller, kept offices in the building.
The Oil City Oil Exchange heavily influenced early crude oil pricing. Brokers there collected 10 cents a barrel from buyers and 5 cents from sellers.

While the Oil City Oil Exchange was the center of the oil industry for nearly two decades, by 1895 Standard Oil had effectively cornered the market. Its chief buyer, Titusville resident Joseph Seep, began paying producers cash directly, at a price Standard set itself. That control lasted until 1911, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark antitrust case that the trust had to be broken into 34 separate companies.
After that, no single company controlled the price of crude oil.
Who sets the price of oil now
Predicting oil prices became a much bigger concern after the oil crises of the 1970s, when sudden price hikes rattled economies around the world.

Today, the price of crude oil is set largely by traders on two exchanges: the New York Mercantile Exchange and the Intercontinental Exchange. Prices there shift from second to second, and gas prices at the pump follow them, usually within days or weeks.

Much of that trading involves futures contracts, which are agreements to buy oil at a set price on a future date. In the U.S., the benchmark contract is for oil delivered to Cushing, Oklahoma, a storage hub where many of the country’s pipelines meet.

The latest shock to that system began this year. War began on Feb. 28, 2026, when the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iranian military targets that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran struck back with missiles and drones and began attacking commercial ships in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean.
Within days, the attacks and a wave of canceled shipping insurance brought tanker traffic nearly to a halt.

On March 2, a Revolutionary Guard commander made the closure official in a statement carried by Iran’s state media: “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If anyone tries to pass, the heroes of the Revolutionary Guards and the regular navy will set those ships ablaze.”
Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through the strait. Most of it goes to Asia, not the U.S. But because oil is traded on a global market, prices rose everywhere.

Oil and gas prices kept climbing as peace talks failed. By May 2026, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was 50% higher than before the war began. Since then, Gulf oil producers have found ways around the blockade, sending oil through pipelines to ports outside the strait and through a U.S.-guarded shipping route near Oman. By late September, those work-arounds had restored about half of the oil that normally passes through the strait, helping keep crude prices around $100 a barrel instead of the much higher levels many analysts had feared.

Oil City’s exchange building is long gone. It was torn down in 1926 to make way for a bank. But the market its traders built, where paper claims on oil change hands far faster than the oil itself moves, still sets what drivers pay at the pump in Oil City and everywhere else.

articles.title: The Holborn and St Pancras byelection doesn’t answer the big questions about British politics – but it provides hints
articles.author: Tony Travers, Professor in Practice, Interim Dean of the LSE School of Public Policy, London School of Economics and Political Science
paras: Holborn and St Pancras is a very unusual constituency. While often referred to as being in “north London”, a significant chunk of it covers the west end, including parts of Covent Garden, Fitzrovia and all of Bloomsbury. It is also home to three of the UK’s largest mainline train stations, two of the three Inns of Court and the British Museum – and, for the time being, the Bayeux Tapestry.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham cracked a good joke at the ceremonial event to launch the tapestry’s visit, speaking of “a leader emerging from a northern territory, travelling to the south of England in search of the crown. Clearly something that couldn’t happen today.”

The byelection was a major test of Burnham’s popularity and his capacity to unite the British centre-left. Labour did remarkably well, with Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali losing just under four percentage points from Keir Starmer’s 2024 vote share. She easily beat the Green party candidate Zack Polanski.

Questions begged at the byelection included: can the “king of the north” appeal to southern voters? Can the Greens win over progressive voters in cities across Britain? Will Conservative and Liberal Democrat supporters vote tactically to keep the Greens out? And has the Green Party of England and Wales been damaged by its conference decision to define Zionism as racism and, effectively, support a policy that would lead to the end of the state of Israel?

Labour’s win clearly showed that Burnham can appeal to London voters. While the city’s media still fear that the prime minister may harbour anti-London sentiments, the Holborn and St Pancras result suggests voters in the capital are prepared to give him a chance.
Battle for Britain’s centre-left

Moreover, after the election became a struggle for the soul of the centre-left, it is possible that the government will now be wary of accidentally sending out anti-London messaging. Labour won 59 out of 75 seats in the capital in 2024, the party’s biggest such concentration in the country. These constituents need to be shown a little love.

The second question has been answered with a resounding “no”. Taking the Green vote in 2024 and adding votes cast for the independent candidate Andrew Feinstein in the same election (a better starting point than just the Green vote), there was a swing of just under 4% from Labour to the Greens.

The Greens can certainly win a proportion of the progressive left vote, but this will not be enough to win many urban seats, even in London. On Thursday’s showing, the party would probably win no seats at all in the city – and few, if any, in similar cities like Leeds, Manchester and Birmingham.

The fall in the Liberal Democrat vote may suggest a modest amount of tactical voting to stop the Greens. In some London borough elections in May this year it looked as if Labour voters switched to the Conservatives to keep Reform UK out. The way Lib Dem, Conservative and Labour supporters use their votes tactically for each other to block the Greens and Reform will be a key feature determining the outcomes of the next general election.

The extent to which the Greens were harmed by their “Zionism is racism” and “one state” policies is impossible to measure. Polling will doubtless help political experts find out more. But the divisions at the top of the party remain, with key figures including its first-ever MP, Caroline Lucas, openly critical of Polanski’s failure to state his position on the issue or to vote at the conference. This does not bode well for the Greens’ capacity to fight the tough and experienced people who run the Labour machine.

The byelection did not answer most of the big questions still facing British politics – notably, is the fragmentation of the “two-party” system starting to reverse? But it gave pointers. Burnham had a good result. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch had a good conference in the same week. For the first time in years, both the Labour and Conservative parties like their leaders and feel optimistic about the future. That this can be said is, of itself, a beguiling curiosity.
